:::{#def-rank-factorization}
#### Rank factorization

Let $\matr{A}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r \ge 1$.
A **rank factorization** of $\matr{A}$ is a product

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{m \times n}
= \underbrace{\matr{C}}_{m \times r}\,\underbrace{\matr{R}}_{r \times n}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-factorization}
#### A rank factorization of a rank-one matrix

The matrix $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space has rank $1$ (@exm-rank-dim), and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 & 1 \cd (-2) & 1 \cd (-2) \\ 3 \cd 1 & 3 \cd (-2) & 3 \cd (-2) \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -6 \end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$

so $\matr{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ ($2 \times 1$)
and $\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ ($1 \times 3$)
are a rank factorization.
It is not unique:
$\matr{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$
and $\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
give the same product.
A product $\matr{C} \matr{R}$ with $\matr{C}$ of size $2 \times 2$
is not a rank factorization of this $\matr{A}$,
because the inner dimension must equal $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = 1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-rank-factorization}
#### Every nonzero matrix has a rank factorization

Every $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ with $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r \ge 1$
has a rank factorization (@def-rank-factorization).
One is given by taking the columns of $\matr{C}$
to be any basis of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.

:::

::: proof

$\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ has dimension $r$ (@thm-rank-dim),
so it has a basis $\vecf{c}_1, \ldots, \vecf{c}_r$ (@thm-extend-basis);
let $\matr{C}$ be the $m \times r$ matrix with these columns.
Each column $\vecf{a}_j$ of $\matr{A}$ is in $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
so $\vecf{a}_j = r_{1j} \vecf{c}_1 + \cdots + r_{rj} \vecf{c}_r$ for some numbers $r_{ij}$,
because the basis spans $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.
Let $\matr{R}$ be the $r \times n$ matrix with entries $r_{ij}$,
whose column $j$ is $\vecf{r}_j = (r_{1j}, \ldots, r_{rj})$.
Then column $j$ of $\matr{C} \matr{R}$ is

$$
\ba
\matr{C} \vecf{r}_j
&= r_{1j} \vecf{c}_1 + \cdots + r_{rj} \vecf{c}_r
&& \text{(@thm-matvec-columns)}
\\
&= \vecf{a}_j,
&& \text{(choice of the } r_{ij} \text{)}
\ea
$$

so $\matr{C} \matr{R} = \matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-factorization-construct}
#### Building a rank factorization from a basis

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space,
$(1, 3)$ spans $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ (@exm-column-space-span),
and it is linearly independent because it is nonzero
($c\,(1, 3) = \vzero_2$ forces $c = 0$),
so it is a basis of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.
The columns of $\matr{A}$ are
$(1, 3) = 1 \cd (1, 3)$,
$(-2, -6) = -2 \cd (1, 3)$ and
$(-2, -6) = -2 \cd (1, 3)$,
so the construction in @thm-rank-factorization gives
$\matr{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$
and $\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$,
the factorization in @exm-rank-factorization.

:::
